primary_topics: Chapter 20 of 'Judicial Renaissance' -- CJP's account of Presidential Commission on Good Government v. Sandiganbayan, a case of first impression in which the Court, by a majority of 11 with two dissents and two non-participations, denied the PCGG's bid to disqualify former Solicitor General Estelito P. Mendoza from representing Lucio Tan and others in the sequestration cases.

The balancing of two policy considerations that the chapter puts at the center: the Court's efforts to upgrade the ethics of lawyers in government service on one hand, and the right of the government to recruit competent counsel to defend its interests on the other.

The majority's reading of Rule 6.03 of the Code of Professional Responsibility through the twin keys of 'matter' and 'intervention' -- advising the Central Bank on how to liquidate GenBank was not the 'matter' the Rule contemplates, and Mendoza's participation was insignificant and insubstantial.

CJP's own Separate Opinion, which would have dismissed the Petition without reaching the ethics question at all -- on conclusiveness of judgment and prescription -- and which proposed that the congruent-interest restriction on former government lawyers expire five years after separation from government service.

The opposing separate opinions: Justice Sandoval-Gutierrez concurring while condemning disqualification motions used to harass, Justice Carpio Morales and Justice Callejo dissenting for a strict application of Rule 6.03, and Justice Tinga denying the Petition on the ground that the Rule could not be applied retroactively.
sub_topics: The opening frame: in this case of first impression the Court found itself choosing between or balancing the upgrading of legal ethics in government service and the government's right to recruit competent counsel.

The facts: on March 25, 1977 the Central Bank declared GenBank insolvent and ordered its liquidation, and Solicitor General Mendoza filed a Petition with the CFI of Manila for the court's assistance and supervision under Section 29 of RA 265.

After the EDSA Revolution of February 1986, President Corazon C. Aquino created the PCGG, which sued to recover alleged ill-gotten wealth and sequestered properties of the Lucio Tan group, by then the owner of GenBank, renamed Allied Banking Corporation.

Mendoza, back in private practice, represented Tan et al. in the Supreme Court petitions to nullify the writs of sequestration, which were referred to the Sandiganbayan Second Division; the PCGG moved to disqualify him under Rule 6.03 for having 'actively intervened' in the liquidation.

The Sandiganbayan Fifth Division denied the disqualification Motion on July 11, 2001, adopting an earlier Second Division Resolution, and denied reconsideration on December 5, 2001, prompting the PCGG's certiorari Petition alleging grave abuse of discretion.

Justice Puno's majority opinion traced Rule 6.03 to the American Bar Association's 1924 concerns about the 'revolving door,' in which lawyers temporarily enter government service and then leave it for large fees in private practice, exploiting information, contacts and influence.

The distinction between an 'adverse-interest conflict' and a 'congruent-interest conflict,' the latter barring a former government lawyer even when the old and new clients' interests are entirely parallel -- the type of conflict alleged against Mendoza.

The meaning of 'matter': per ABA Formal Opinion No. 342, drafting, enforcing or interpreting government procedures, regulations or laws, or briefing abstract principles, is not a 'matter,' and the liquidation proceeding differed entirely from the sequestration cases.

The meaning of 'intervention': of the two readings, the Court adopted the narrower one confined to acts of a person with power to influence the proceedings, and found Mendoza's signing of an initiatory pleading and unclear participation insignificant and insubstantial.

The policy balance: Rule 6.03 must not chill government recruitment of able legal talent, must not become a litigation tactic to harass opposing counsel and deprive a client of the lawyer in whom it has confidence, and must not compromise the official independence or the professional freedom of government lawyers.

The majority's disposal of the remaining rationales -- appearance of impropriety already abandoned by the 1983 ABA Model Rules, no 'switching sides' because the liquidation and the sequestration differed in subject matter, no conflict of loyalties, and the concern over former officials' clout dismissed as overextended and demeaning.

CJP's Separate Opinion: there was no need to inquire whether Rule 6.03 had been transgressed, because the April 22, 1991 Resolution of the Sandiganbayan Second Division on the same disqualification issue between the same parties had become final and immutable.

His statement of the estoppel rule that for conclusiveness of judgment to operate, the only identity required is that between parties and issues, even though the main claims for reversion, reconveyance and restitution remained unadjudicated.

His proposal on prescription: the congruent-interest restriction should expire after a reasonable period when no further prejudice to the public could be contemplated -- five years from retirement or separation, the prescriptive period for suits for which no period is fixed by law -- since a perpetual and absolute ban would be unduly harsh, unreasonable and unfair.

The Gutierrez Concurring Opinion: motions to disqualify counsel deserve caution because they may be filed to harass, delay, intimidate or gain tactical advantage, and the PCGG's 'scattershot manner' of filing showed intent to harass; she also held the denial final and appealable, res judicata applicable, and the two proceedings different in parties, issues, facts and reliefs.

The Morales Dissenting Opinion: conclusiveness of judgment does not apply to issues of law when substantially unrelated claims are involved (Kilosbayan v. Morato), a five-year cap is unacceptable, privileged communication outlives the attorney-client relationship, and what mattered was Mendoza's role in facilitating the liquidation through his legal expertise.

The Callejo Dissenting Opinion: a strict application of Rule 6.03 is needed as an ethical compass and to avoid the appearance of impropriety; Mendoza's acts were discrete, isolatable, identifiable transactions and hence a 'matter,' his role was significant per the March 29, 1977 Central Bank Memorandum, and the absence of a temporal limitation in the Rule was deliberate.

The Tinga Separate Opinion: Rule 6.03 had not yet been promulgated when Mendoza entered government service, so applying it would violate his right to due process and set a dangerous precedent of retroactive application of a source of penal liabilities binding only on Philippine Bar Association members at the time.

stances.claim: The Petition should have been dismissed without inquiring whether Rule 6.03 had been transgressed, because the Sandiganbayan's April 22, 1991 Resolution resolving the very same disqualification ground between the same parties had become final and immutable.
stances.rhetorical_move: procedural pre-emption -- resolving the case on conclusiveness of judgment so the Court need not pronounce on a contested ethical question at all

stances.claim: For conclusiveness of judgment to operate as an estoppel, the only identity required is that between parties and issues, so the absence of a final adjudication on the main claims of reversion, reconveyance and restitution does not revive the settled disqualification question.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal precision -- isolating the elements of the estoppel to show that what remains unlitigated is irrelevant to what has been conclusively settled

stances.claim: The restriction on former government lawyers under congruent-interest representation should expire five years from retirement or separation from government service, five years being the prescriptive period for suits for which no period is prescribed by law.
stances.rhetorical_move: analogical borrowing from prescription law plus a fairness appeal -- a perpetual and absolute ban on lawyers who once served the government would be unduly harsh, unreasonable and unfair

stances.claim: A too-strict Rule 6.03 would chill the government's recruitment of able legal talent, invite the litigation tactic of harassing opposing counsel, and deprive former government lawyers of the freedom to exercise their profession.
stances.rhetorical_move: reported as the majority's balancing of competing policy considerations, with the ethical aim weighed against its institutional costs

stances.claim: Rule 6.03 should be applied strictly to provide an ethical compass to lawyers and to avoid even the appearance of impropriety, and the absence of an explicit temporal limitation in the Rule was deliberate.
stances.rhetorical_move: reported position of the Callejo dissent, argued from the discrete and identifiable character of Mendoza's acts and from Canon 36's policy against the appearance of evil

notable_anecdotes: CJP notes the unusual vote count in a case of first impression: eleven members forming the majority, two dissenting, and two taking no part in the deliberations and voting.

He records that he pointedly declined to join either side's ethical reasoning -- Puno's that the advice was not a 'matter,' Callejo's that the Rule had been violated -- submitting with due respect that there was no need to inquire into the Rule at all.

He recounts the origin of the concern behind Rule 6.03 in the American Bar Association's 1924 worry about the 'revolving door,' where lawyers enter government briefly and leave for large fees in private practice.
He quotes Justice Sandoval-Gutierrez's finding that the 'scattershot manner' in which the PCGG filed its various motions to disqualify Atty. Mendoza showed an intent to harass him and Tan et al.

He reports Justice Carpio Morales's riposte to the recruitment argument -- that financial considerations are not the sole factor in attracting lawyers to government, because serving in the government is its own reward.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 20 of 'Judicial Renaissance' recounts Presidential Commission on Good Government v. Sandiganbayan, which Panganiban presents as a case of first impression forcing the Court to balance its drive to upgrade the ethics of lawyers in government service against the government's right to recruit competent counsel. The PCGG had moved to disqualify Atty. Estelito P. Mendoza, solicitor general when the Central Bank declared GenBank insolvent in March 1977, from representing Lucio Tan and others in the sequestration cases over Allied Banking Corporation, invoking Rule 6.03 of the Code of Professional Responsibility against accepting engagement in any matter in which a lawyer had intervened while in government service. The Sandiganbayan denied the Motion, and by a majority of eleven, with two dissents and two non-participations, the Court denied the PCGG's certiorari Petition. Justice Puno's ponencia traced the Rule to the ABA's 1924 concern with the 'revolving door,' distinguished adverse-interest from congruent-interest conflicts, and held that advising the Central Bank on liquidation procedure was not the 'matter' the Rule contemplates and that Mendoza's participation -- signing an initiatory pleading -- was insignificant and insubstantial; it also warned against chilling government recruitment and against disqualification used as a harassment tactic. Panganiban wrote separately to dismiss the Petition only on conclusiveness of judgment and prescription, arguing that the Sandiganbayan's final April 22, 1991 Resolution on the identical ground had become immutable, that identity of parties and issues alone suffices for estoppel, and that the congruent-interest restriction should expire five years after separation from government, since a perpetual and absolute ban would be unduly harsh, unreasonable and unfair. He reports Justice Sandoval-Gutierrez's concurrence condemning the PCGG's 'scattershot' motions, Justice Carpio Morales's dissent rejecting both conclusiveness of judgment and the five-year cap, Justice Callejo's dissent urging strict application as an ethical compass, and Justice Tinga's view that applying a rule promulgated after Mendoza entered government would violate his right to due process.
